comments.name: Crystal Clear

At the same time gun ownership, mass shootings, stand your ground laws, and highly publicized incidents of policy brutality further a culture of aggressiveness and devaluation of our shared humanity. Basic psychology tells us that this kind of heavy handed “discipline” brought to bear on school children (whose brains and social emotional abilities are still developing) will be more harmful than beneficial. Read this article in the context of other reporting by the NYT on the still legal use of corporal punishment in schools in many states, the forced shaving of hair and other racially and culturally stereotyped discrimination and I can’t help but worry about the purpose this is meant to serve. The educators I know, in my family and beyond, would not call this pedagogy.

comments.name: Ernie
comments.body:
In the middle on this one. I live in Oakland, where students are allowed to act out, defy teachers, threaten, and engage in violence. We have some of the worst public schools in California.  The private schools just expel after the second incident.  We have great charter schools.

Kid got a gun in a backpack. Yes, I want criminal arrest.  Kid bumps into counselor on purpose, I want action.  Not words. One strike allowed, #2 and bye bye.  This isn't just a "justice" issue, it's also a fight for schools that can teach kids that desperately need a safe place to learn in.

comments.name: Zinnia
comments.body: I was assaulted by a fellow student when I was in junior high. Fortunately, I was not severely injured. Unbeknownst to me or my parents, the girl who assaulted me had a history of violent behavior and had been expelled from two other schools before she arrived at mine. Following the incident, she was expelled a third time. I don’t know what happened to her but she was not arrested. Obviously she was not arrested…she was only 12 years old! She had a serious rage problem that required mental health treatment (such as it was then; this happened over 50 years ago), not juvenile detention. I hope she got help. No one at the time, not my parents, not the school authorities, ever floated the idea that the police needed to be involved.

comments.name: Paula Kirkham
comments.body:
As a social worker who many years ago worked on the streets and in the homes of juvenile offenders we had a rule of thumb:

You only get one chance to use arrest/detention as a motivator for behavioral change. Once a kid has their first experience with arrest/detention the fear of same is replaced by actual experience. They learn a thing or two: they learn they can survive it; they meet other offenders (often seriously disturbed offenders involved in significant criming) and form relationships with them that carry on after release from detention, often resulting in increased negative->illegal behaviors; the fear of the unknown is replaced by knowledge of how to work the system.

You only get one shot. Texas is blowing it.

comments.name: Audacity
comments.body: I find this abhorrent but also expected. The problem begins with elementary schools that fail to discipline and intervene early. My 2nd female grader was hit by several boys - one kicked her in the stomach and back. The school did nothing. The boy had previously caused another girl to break bones. The school did nothing. This was at a top rated school with a wealthy population. This is not an isolated case, several boys had physically assaulted other kids without discipline. This is happening in schools with less resources as well. The children are being allowed to continue this behavior with no discipline, so of course when they get to an age where they can go to juvi- the answer is lock them up. It should have been earlier intervention and resources, but there is no funding for that. On top of it, they have introduced screens for several hours a day that makes disciplining more difficult. It’s horrendous. I have to homeschool my daughter to give her a good education in a safe environment. The Governor sold out our public schools with the private school voucher system. That’s why I am voting for Gina. I’m tired of our educational systems falling apart.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
Here in California we have the opposite problem.

We are not allowed to give students any consequences! There is no detention, no reflection time, and definitely never suspension or expulsion. You can't even have a student pick up trash as a consequence.

In most cases, the parents don't know what to do and are begging us to give their children consequences, but the schools say they hands are tied.

Obviously this leads to disruptive classrooms where no one learns anything, and good teachers quit the profession.

Please bring back discipline!

By that I mean that every action he takes results in the opposite reaction that he intends. If that is the case, deporting Ilhan Omar to Somalia might be the single most globally important act of his Presidency. What if she manages to stabilize and unite everything from Yemen to the Kenyan border, and win the Nobel Peace Prize in the process? comments.name: Nga
comments.body: Oh my goodness, I could not believe what I was reading in the NYT, the NYT!  This is wrong on so many levels, and I sincerely cannot understand the reason why reporting resources were sent out on this boondoggle story of a backyard breeder (who got thousands of dollars of free PR here).  I agree with many of the readers who pointed out the lack of understanding and engagement with more important matters in the world of animal interest and welfare.  One of our local Shelter dogs here in Santa Cruz County just got selected as "Chief Snuggle Officer" in the Purina National Contest a few days ago!  It's not about sad rescues and depressing shelters, it about educating the public and increasing awareness.  It's about the celebration of love, heroism, and the transformational connection of humans and animals and the natural world.  Please NYT do better, y'all got fleeced on this one!

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: We are on our sixth rescue in 39 years of marriage. And they rescued us ... and taught us a lot. I'm reminded of Marcus, our third, a Skipperke mix who was tied up in a backyard with three other dogs and all attacked by killer bees. Two of the dogs died. Marcus was stung innumerable times and had to have an eye removed. Maybe a compromised liver. But he made it through, he was tough and OMG, sweet. We had him for gosh, 15 years(?), and he lived life to the fullest: still doing zoomies in the backyard the day before he passed. And he never knew he only had one eye (he was an expert at peering around corners). He taught us to do the best with the hand we're dealt. Miss him.

comments.name: Tom Boyhan
comments.body:
The best dog I've ever seen was a Border Collie named Walrus owned by a fellow SEAL teammate.
On a visit to his property we took a canoe out on the water. Gary put Walrus in a down/stay as we pushed off leaving Walrus on shore. We were gone for about hour when we realized the tide was coming in. When we got back Walrus was still in place with the water lapping at his front paws. I believe that dog would have held his position until he was floating! Gary had many stories of Walrus working as a cattle dog in the Chilcotin area of British Columbia. While the dog was an outstanding work dog it also was relaxed in the home setting. Truly an amazing animal.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body:
Lovely story. We got a Boston Terrier puppy a bit over a year ago. He has been a joy and a challenge. But at age 78 and feeble, he was the best choice for us. Low maintenance, and with a huge backyard he gets plenty of exercise. He is totally bonded with us, and a huge emotional support for our oldest daughter who lives with us. She takes him for walks and plays with him in ways we cannot. 

Candidly, I did not want a dog. I feared we could not handle one. It is sometimes hard, to be sure, but the love and joy he has brought have made it all worthwhile. We donate a lot now to animal rescue and animal protection causes. My wife would adopt 20 rescue dogs if she could. Then again, she is insane. /s

Fox collies sound like really great, really cute dogs. If we didn't have our great little guy, one would be a superb choice for us.

comments.name: Melissa Sterrett Baron
comments.body: Over the last 20 years I have had the great pleasure to live with some of the best dogs in the world as our family companions. I started off with Rhodesian Ridgebacks, and I thought they were the greatest breed created. Next up was a half-Ibizan, half-Ridgeback hound that was an accidental pairing from an ethical breeder. She was an amazing dog—so smart, so sweet, so intelligent. Once the shelters were overflowing, it became clear that rescued needed to be my new breed. So along came an amazing Pittie-Staffy-Doberman-Boxer mix. He is now one of my two latest, greatest loves. My point here? There is no one perfect dog; they all are!

There are four things people need to "get ahead" - I call them the Four Aspirants - the things people with less than median income need to thrive and these should be made affordable to people with less than median income:  transportation, health care, higher education and housing. In all my years of reading Mr. Asimov's musings on wine, both practical and philosophical (and his running of Wine School as well), I remain grateful for his skill at bringing the world of wine to life for us.

This piece in particular strikes a deep chord with me. I grew up in a large Italian family where wine was always part of the meal, both in our home and at my relatives' homes, and I learned a great deal about it from my family as a young man.

When I returned as an adult years later, my uncle—who worked as an importer—discovered I was learning as much as I could about wine on my own and brought me down to his cellar to show me some older bottles he had stashed away. He pulled out and opened a 25-year-old Amarone.

What struck me most about that moment was that we did not talk about the wine at all. Instead, he shared memories about his time in Italy, where he was stationed as a Marine just after WWII, how he met my aunt there, how he came to appreciate wine, and how he turned that passion into a career importing wines and spirits from Europe. He had never spoken of this before—it was a real treat to hear his stories.

The article makes brief references to a lot of what goes on in Israel that is never covered in the US media or social media, and it would be interesting to know more. I hope that Mr. Abbas stays safe and can help to form the government that Israel needs. Being a peace-maker draws a lot of enemies.

comments.name: Nick Eliopulos
comments.body: it’s interesting that in the US he is low profile and there isn’t a movement a stronger more public movement to back his approach.

comments.name: N Ba
comments.body: This what exposure and experience with the democratic process is all about. His current position would have been unthinkable in his own lifetime. I hope his faith in the democratic process is rewarded with positive results.

comments.name: Ruth Roded
comments.body: Let’s give credit to the Arab citizens of Israel who according to polls will be voting in unprecedented numbers and will win about 15/120 members of the parliament. I wouldn’t put it past any so-called Jewish party to ally with them to get power. Neither the Netanyahu coalition nor the anti Netanyahu coalition have enough to form a government without the two Arab parties (which you confused in the article)

comments.name: Ben
comments.body: If any Palestinian Arab politicians have taken the harder, necessary road, it is those of the Hadash and the Joint List. It is a mistake to write them off, as this article does by implication.

comments.name: Progressive American
comments.body:
Arab Israelis really need to enter politics with the idea of wielding power, not rejecting all coordination with other political parties and the whole concept of Israeli government. It's uncomfortable, and the Arab world might condemn them for it, but they're the ones who actually live in Israel.

You can't gain power in a Parliamentary system if you don't form coalitions with other parties. 

The Haredim (probably less popular than Arabs with most Israeli Jews) have done this masterfully. All they care about is getting government welfare handouts and avoiding military service, and they get those things by joining coalitions. 

If Arab parties followed suit, they really would be kingmakers. I mean, they are 20 percent of the electorate.

articles.title: The Arab Kingmaker in Israel’s Election Who Wants a Partnership With Jews
articles.byline: David M. Halbfinger and Adam Rasgon
articles.summary: Mansour Abbas, a dentist-turned-lawmaker, helped oust Benjamin Netanyahu once before. Now, he and a Jewish ex-police commander have teamed up to try to do it again.

comments.name: Joanne
comments.body:
I love the 1995 version of Sense and Sensibility. It had two of my very favorite actors, Alan Rickman and Robert Hardy, who were wonderful. That scene when Col Brandon walks into the house to hear Marianne playing and singing with his eyes riveted on her affects me like I’ve never seen it before, every time. Do I think Rickman could ever be improved upon? No, probably not. 

But here’s the thing - I’m going to see this new movie with an open mind to find out what it’s like. I truly dislike the attitude of “I’m not going to see it because I don’t like their hair/it’s not muddy enough/it’s too muddy/it can never be bettered/I don’t like the actor who plays Elinor.” 

It’s like saying, I love Restaurant A and therefore I won’t try any other restaurant because it could never be better. You’re basing your opinion on a 2 minute trailer, word of mouth, and a movie review. 

I think anything else is just stubbornness.

comments.name: Bridgman
comments.body: It is hard for me to imagine any other version capturing the wit and depth of Thompson's. And who could replace supporting players like Gemma Jones, Robert Hardy, Imelda Staunton, Alan Rickman, et al? Also the Patrick Doyle's magnificent score had much to do with the aforementioned depth. That version was an oil painting, this looks like a snapshot.

comments.name: Anne Ellen
comments.body: The music is awful.

comments.name: Pria
comments.body:
One of the Indian Sense and Sensibility
Adaptation is fresh, gorgeously filmed with great songs by AR Rahman. It is called Kandukondein Kandukondein.

comments.name: C M Cherce
comments.body: Someone explain this odd-reading sentence in the review--"As with wildlife, well-bred women who have lost their fortunes find their lives dictated by mercurial forces..."

comments.name: Terrierdem
comments.body: Austen household even in genteel poverty had two maids and a manservant. Women of their class would not be chopping wood, nor would they be seen with unkempt hair. The composers of this film should have done some research on the era in which Miss Austen and her ilk lived. Maybe check out Lucy Worley and Dan Snows’ conversations on Jane Austen and her times.

comments.name: B.
comments.body: What exactly is “realistic” about making a version that does not respect historical context ? The further directors depart from the Austen text the less culturally accurate the film becomes. What’s clearly getting on people’s nerves is this assertion by the director that her uninformed view of what was to live in the Regency times has any sort of historical validity. Viewers have no problem with fantasy versions of the past, look at the success of Bridgeton, and S&S is fiction after all, but everyone needs to know what exactly are the rules of this “universe”.

comments.name: S
comments.body: Really great review!

articles.summary: A lush new adaptation of Jane Austen’s novel leans into youth and money troubles.

comments.name: Dante
comments.body: My first thoughts were 'why was this animal never tranquilized and transported to a herd on the mainland?' and my second thought was how lonely that beast must've been at times, and how selfish human beings are when they view a wild animal as some sort of a pet.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: Male elks go off on their own, hoping to make their way in the world and mate. It's disheartening he never did the latter.

comments.name: JJ
comments.body: I believe he was swimming in the Salish Sea and got carried away by a current.

comments.name: John

comments.name: kkseattle

comments.name: Jorosa
comments.body: I don’t blame him for escaping to an island. Every time I read the news I want to do the same thing.

comments.name: Whip or Will
comments.body: Great piece.  Thank you.

articles.title: Bruiser the Elk Left His Herd for an Island and Made It Home
articles.summary: After swimming across chilly waters to Whidbey Island in Washington State, the solitary elk charmed residents for more than a decade with his antics. He died at 15 to 18 years old.

comments.name: Inarasj
comments.body: I actually had dinner here a long time ago.  I had found the restaurant in a National Geographic article before my trip.  Food and service we excellent!

comments.name: Andy Humm
comments.body: Yes, I did almost break a tooth on the buckshot in my grouse--failing to heed the warning on the menu. I don't see the Stilton soup on the menu but hope it comes back. Same for the rack of lamb. The public school desserts are always fun. And Rules is always worth a visit--even if you are by yourself at one of their cozy tables.

comments.name: NWC
comments.body: It seems clear from the comments that the food has improved since we lived in London in the 1960’s. The atmosphere is outstanding and generally it was a memorable experience. Especially the dessert which was fresh raspberries with a jug of cream. The raspberries were moldy and when the (not English) waiter was apprised of the fact he was unmoved. “The English are very crafty” he said, bearing a punnet of raspberries. “They are beautiful on top but underneath they are moldy.”

comments.name: George AdScam Parker
comments.body: If you go, make sure you book a table on the ground floor. The second floor dining room is a somewhat sparse area with much less atmosphere.

comments.name: JohnT
comments.body: A much more comprehensive article than that of The Times of London - well done!  As an expat Brit who dined there whilst working in London, but who now lives in Montana, it was a bittersweet read - I immediately wanted to call and book a table.  The article well catches the culinary, social and historical atmosphere, and also its comfortable egalitarian feel.  However, it is still possible to celebrity spot the rich and famous - on one occasion a Government Minister and his extremely young female companion.  I gave him the benefit of the doubt, supposing it could have been his niece, especially remembering the looks I had when I had treated my extremely pretty teenage goddaughter to lunch when she was visiting town.  The Press later revealed that my 'benefit of the doubt' was misplaced.

comments.name: David
comments.body: My acadian uncles in Canada hunted game regularly and they were busily employed by the railroad and local paper mill.   One uncle would transport illegally hunted deer to your house for a price.  Moose meat was a treat delivered to my mother from her brothers.  Another husband of my first cousin ( a native who could hunt out of season) would deliver salmon to his mother in law, my god mother, but he had to sit at table while it was eaten as was the demand of Canadian law.  For Canadians , the Rules governing hunting game are much different.

comments.name: Genghis Lapointe
comments.body: I ate there once, in 1999. Maybe it was because I was alone and didn't spend enough on my dinner, but before I was done the waiter told me he was anxious to have the table. I would never return.

comments.name: Paco

comments.name: Disillusioned Lefty
comments.body:
All this analysis about how bonds for the long run makes sense, in fact makes no sense. Look at debt-to-GDP. It was fairly tame and under control until 2008, and then just kept climbing at a steady pace, with no moderation in sight and absolutely no political will to fix the problems. 

Inflation in real terms is an overspending problem. Your bonds will just erode in value starting from the moment you buy them. It’s a mug’s game, a pure suckers bet. Real assets represent the only hope of fighting the long-term debasement of your money. Anyone who tells you different is a liar.

comments.name: Barbara Barran
comments.body: Israeli bonds are paying higher interest rates than US ones, and they are very safe. My family has invested in them for over half a century.

comments.name: M
comments.body: We’re going to get downgraded again

comments.name: Scott
comments.body:
After 40+ years of investing, my approach to bonds is this: (1) Buy and hold to maturity, (2) Buy only bonds, stay away from bond funds or ETFs, (3) build a bond ladder.

Doing this makes you immune to interest rate fluctuations which cause price fluctuations. As long as you hold to maturity, that bond will retain its face value and you will not lose any principal. Just keep racking in the coupon payments and when it matures, buy more bonds and hold those to maturity. Higher interest rates are not a risk, they are a huge benefit in this scheme because your return is entirely due to interest. But my approach is that stocks are for growth and bonds are for security so I am pretty happy with the greater predictability of buying and holding bonds.

comments.name: Richard Wachterman
comments.body: "That means that bond buyers who sell before their bonds mature could face short-term losses." If you sell your bonds before they mature (and invest in bonds with higher interest rates), or hold your bonds to maturity, the resulting loss is the same.

comments.body:
How incredibly near-sighted.  Cheering higher interest rates as some sort of investment "opportunity" is like cheering the arrival of firetrucks outside your house.

Until you ask why they're there.

comments.name: A
comments.body: Mr. Sommer has it right. Yet Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading left-wing presidential candidate in France, advocates simply cancelling payment on bonds. That's a risk that, one hopes, is unlikely in the U.S. But it's a proposal which will appeal to irresponsible politicians on both right and left because it sounds cost-free. comments.name: Magisterludi

comments.name: gordon
comments.body:
The democrats won’t win because they’re democrats, they’ll win because they’re not republicans, and more specifically, they’re not the party of Trump. I don’t think there’s a pundit or political analyst or election analyst alive who doesn’t know this. Surely the democrats themselves know this. 

But winning this midterm isn’t the end of anything, it’s the start of something else. It will put the winning democrats in the spotlight where they will either fish or cut bait, and I’m honestly holding my breath with worry.

comments.name: Gowan McAvity
comments.body: There is never any one person in charge when the party in opposition, with at least the presidency occupied by the other party, especially when both Senate and House also in the majority along with the president, when the midterms occur. The party that is still being lead by the losing candidate from the last election, in such a rout, or even a close election, will most often lose, and a successor won’t be named until the primaries define one after the midterms. The people chose the party leader through election. When someone is anointed by the establishment, something democracy abhors, the result is the last election. Deserved defeat.

comments.name: Frustrated Democrat
comments.body: Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are the most significant liabilities to the Democratic Party.  Both are both too focused on bipartisanship and "gentlemen politics." Just last month Jeffries and Jared Kushner held a private meeting in New York to discuss potential bipartisan issues. Jeffries has rarely called out Mike Johnson by name, and he is not the "fighter" we need leading the House. And Schumer is nearly 76 years old, hunched over and weary. He no longer has the "fight" in him. Both Jeffries and Schumer need to step down from their leadership positions after the midterms. Replace Schumer with Ossoff or Slotkin or Murphy.  These are the type of leaders we need in positions of power. They are not passive. Even if Democrats win the House and Senate in the midterms, we need bold, forceful, strategic, vocal, media savvy leadership to repair some of the devastation inflicted by Trump and his Republican Congress.  Schumer and Jeffries are not capable.

comments.name: Jeff T
comments.body:
The Democratic Party cannot “reform” itself…

Capitalism in the U.S. has been effectively unconstrained for decades (long before *Citizens United*).

A major reason is that wealthy interests have bought government and BOTH political parties.

There is no question that GOP trickle-down economic policies have led to unsustainable levels of wealth and income inequality in the country, and made it virtually ungovernable.

However, after the Great Recession of 2008, virtually no Wall Street executives were prosecuted and money center banks were bailed out with taxpayer money. Taxpayers, all Americans, small businesses got no help - nothing.

If the United States is to survive it will only be through a new New Deal for all Americans. 

In my humble opinion, I don’t think the Democratic Party can carry this forward AND sustain it. 

We need new political parties. And no, I don’t think they’re likley to arise in time. But if not, Adios.

comments.name: Steve

I fear that the far left / Socialist side of the party will be extreme enough the next 1-2 years to scare independents.

comments.name: Aging Fast
comments.body:
I understand the recommendation to move to more orally based forms of evaluation.  But I worry that those allow for many forms of biases to affect the evaluation even more than they do now.

The future in scholarly fields - including math - will be learning to work with AI to produce research (perhaps by rewriting or reformulating what’s in computer code).   Evaluation should be about the ability to engage in that collaboration.

comments.name: joe
comments.body: As an engineer, math is just another tool to solve problems, not much different from using a word processor to communicate. I see better more efficient tools as a positive.

comments.name: Bob Cox
comments.body: The goal of academic progress is to increase understanding. In pure math, that is particularly true. Solving problems is part of that, but generating new problems is a different skill entirely. Creating entire new classes of mathematical thought is yet a different level of achievement. At present, no AI is capable of the latter. Could AI invent analytic number theory, as Riemann did in 1859? Could AI invent complex analysis as Cauchy did in the 1820s? Both creations were new ways of thinking and perceiving mathematical issues. AI can absorb all of the literature about these, better than any human (even Terry Tao), and churn out advances along the lines of already existing thought. But going outside of the well trodden paths - that is not for every PhD mathematician, and is definitely not yet for LLMs.

comments.name: Canadian
comments.body:
It's a terrible tragedy. Math is one of our oldest and most illustrious of human creative endeavors. As AI can solve the most complex math problems we can think of, it fundamentally changes what a math problem even is to begin with. What will math graduate students do? What will a career in math look like?

What does math as a discipline even mean anymore, when math problems disappear entirely?

When AI replaces human thinking, what will people who think for a living do?

comments.name: AaronS
comments.body:
We will always need higher-order mathematicians to alert us when there are flaws in what AI has produced.

I used AI regularly to create multiple-choice questions, etc., from various articles, etc.  Often, I (or my students) find questions where they a correct answer is not even a provided option.  That's why you need someone who ACTUALLY knows the material.  Otherwise, we risk students being raised to think that incorrect information is correct.

comments.name: Here
comments.body:
AI is good for mathematics, bad for mathematicians.

But that is true for all human endeavors: AI is good for human life, bad for humans.

If humans devolved back to an early state of not understanding higher math, but AI continues to progress on its own and creates a world in which humans thrive -- much like dogs thrive as pets under human care and munificence and love -- is that a bad thing?

Is it bad that dogs don't do algebra? They live a perfectly content and satisfying life under the roof of another species that, truth be told, a vast majority of can't do algebra either!

It’s a joke on us and we are just AI’s pets, like dogs who can’t understand what is being said. comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
The problem with these biological age tests are that the data is incomplete. There is population evidence associating these scores with all cause, cardiovascular and cancer deaths. But, the details aren't really worked out. So, in any individual the results are difficult to interpret and not standardized among the different tests.

More importantly, because these Silicon Valley start up folks are looking to make a quick buck. So, instead of doing follow up studies to assess what interventions can be done (there are no studies showing any type of intervention can effectively affect your aging rate/mortality), they just go direct to consumer to sell a product for a quick buck. 

The problem is there is no return on your health care investment if you spend money on these at this time. They need to hammer out the details with further studies to show what meaningful interventions can be done based on these scores. 

As another reader noted, the best case use, sadly, for these tests and other genetic testing at this time, is that it gives insurance entities the ability to assess risk further and exclude high risk individuals. Somewhat of a dubious achievement...

comments.name: Grunt
comments.body: Look no farther than Apple’s approach. It determined that 90% of use cases can be handled by local, on device AI, with the remaining 10% farmed out to external, cloud AI powered by Gemini or, in the future, some other provider. Its Mac Studios and Minis are flying off the shelf because of this verified thesis—they are currently the best value for running AI locally. A used M4 Mac Mini on eBay costs more than what it cost when it was bought new.  This is especially important for enterprises. Having a Mac Studio or Mini on everyone’s desks to handle 70-90% of AI prompts and farming out only 10-30% to providers represent huge savings, not to mention data security and privacy. Data centers and GPUs are being bought by hyperscalers as if everyone will be tapping into cloud AI for most of their needs. NVidia continues to push this business model for obvious reasons, but even it is hedging by introducing desktop PCs, similar to Mac Studios and Minis, for customers to run AI locally. Unfortunately, its fortunes still come from server scale GPUs, so to keep the bubble inflated, it’s funding the AI labs and hyperscalers with equity investments in exchange for their GPU purchases—converting equity into illusory revenues, which gives them an instant market value boost because the market values revenues at a multiple of the equity investment amount that funded it. comments.name: DJS

After reading this below, I can not figure out how any Texan would vote for this man? Have we not learned from dealing with Trump what a mistake putting him in power has been?  Vote the person,  NOT the party!  Integrity matters!

Quote from article:

There’s a reason Paxton and his allies have clawed at every possible advantage. He’s got baggage to spare. During a quarter-century in Texas politics, he has never lost an election. But as attorney general, he was charged with felony fraud. He cut a deal to drop the charges in exchange for paying restitution and performing community service. Then, a group of his aides accused him of bribery and abuse of office. The lower house of the state legislature impeached him in 2023. (The upper house acquitted him.) comments.name: Jacqui
comments.body:
My spouse and I are overseas Texas voters. My spouse naturalized as a US citizen in the 1980s, and has voted in every election since. We moved to Texas in the early 1990s, then to Germany in the 2010s. We have witnessed firsthand the downfall of the DEM party in Texas and the subsequent despair accompanied by it. But we are cautiously optimistic this time.
 First off, although we send in our voter renewals annually, my spouse's voter registration was delayed due to the extra scrutiny ordered on naturalized citizens. After that hurdle was crossed, we learned some central post handlers in the state were closed, supposedly to cut costs, and saw our mail slow to a crawl. A letter sent to me, franked on August 24, just arrived in my post yesterday, October 16th!!! We mailed our ballots in on Oct 5, the day after we received them. At this rate, I'm not sure they will be sorted in Texas on time to count. Emailed ballots are not an option. If Talarico and/or more DEMs win than are expected by the state GOP after the gerrymandering they did this cycle, I can't help but wonder what the president and the state will do. We have to be prepared. Texas, for the first time since the '90s, is the canary in the coal mine.

comments.name: thenewguy

Some of the comments here focus too much on the two people concerned, and forget that many voters think "vote for the team, not the person" when they're at the ballot box.  If you're hardcore MAGA, Paxton will be a reliable Yes vote for Trump in the senate.  They could despise him personally, but still vote for him and be rational (within the confines of that decision, let's say).  
To be clear, I don't support it, but it explains why such a flawed candidate could still be elected.

comments.name: Jack Dempsey
comments.body: The massive investments into AI chips are based on the idea a huge increase in compute will yield similar improvements to the LLM AI models the previous increases in compute gave. MIT recently released a paper dismissing that idea. The AI model improvements will hard cap out soon, and they will not give the same improvements in performance they gave before. As someone who studied AI and computer science, I could see the brute force way LLMs process data will hit Moore's Law very soon and the MIT paper agrees. I'm guessing the scientists at these AI companies know this too, but are relying on the "exponential to infinity" hysteria and circular financing to boost their valuations and personally try to cash out as much as they can before reality hits hype. I doubt many of the mega data centres will get built before the financial pyramid built on sand collapses.

comments.name: Mara
comments.body: I believe the life of every human being's life should be protected no matter what the person has done. Killing a person cannot be justified. Every person deserves the chance to live and be forgiven. The idea of executing someone because they have killed someone makes everything our country has done to become what it is completely shatter.

comments.name: Aziza
comments.body: I don't really have a thought on the death penalty. I believe that all actions have consequences, good or bad.  I think that felons should have time to reflect on their actions and pay for what they did; however, I think that death should not be an option. But rather that punishments should be given.

comments.name: Nick c
comments.body: I believe the death penalty should still be in use in the United States. There are many cases in which someone does something so inhumane that they should be treated accordingly. If a dog bites a baby and cannot be fixed, it gets put down. I believe the same should apply to humans. For example, if someone consistently murders people not in self -defense or commits other atrocious actions such as rape, they should be put to death. It even states in the bible, that the punishment for rape is death.

comments.name: Yasir
comments.body: I believe that the death penalty should be used in extreme crimes, such as Murder, terrorism, etc. I believe the people who do these crimes should get the death penalty because it is going to increase the safety. Also if you use regular prison sentences after a while they will just get out, and reek more havoc, but I also believe that it should not be livestreamed as it normalizes murder, and it should be pain free to be as humaine.

comments.name: Makayla
comments.body: I believe that the death penalty is an extreme punishment that should no longer be in effect. I think it is unethical and while many criminals do deserve punishment, there are other ways to give severe punishment. At times, its better so a bad human being to be locked up and suffer slowly rather than not have their lives at all in an instant. While this is a hard topic for me as I can see how many do deserve death penalty, I think my emotions can get in the way of feeling bad for them.

comments.name: Elias Shishani
comments.body: I support the use of the death penalty. I support its use because at some point people need to realize some people are incapable of being rehabilitated and wasting funds to keep someone who will never be fit to return to society fed and housed is not worth while. Some people may argue that the death penalty is barbaric or inhumane but I believe that it isn’t. One reason I believe the death penalty isn't inhumane is because the means of execution has changed massively from going from beheadings and hangings to lethal injections. Another reason I don’t find an issue with the death penalty isn't because I believe that the type of person to be sentenced to capital punishment are not deserving of being treated fairly as they often commit cruel crimes that lead to death of innocent people. A fair argument against the death penalty that I sometimes see is that is that people can be wrongfully convicted and it can be used maliciously by the government to legally kill those who speak against them. This is a problem that I see no easy solution to and the only solution I could think of is to make the process for someone to be sentenced to death to be very extensive and leave very little room for wrongful convictions. In the end I think the death penalty should still be used while it has issues with it that need to be addressed it can provide benefits and is another thing to discourage those who think of committing crimes.

comments.name: Maeve L
comments.body: I argue that the Death Penalty should no longer be used in the Untied States. It is an extreme punishment that is inhumane and reflects poorly on our morals as the Untied States. Jeremy Engle reports that the livestream of the execution of a gunman involved in a mass shooting is having people question the existence of the death penalty in the Untied States. It is important to recognize the severity of the death penalty and the family’s behind the incarcerated person who have known this person all their lives. Although there are unforgivable and despicable crimes they should be met with the sentence of live in prison not their death.

comments.name: Tristan Zamudio
comments.location: Glenbard West HS, Glen Ellyn IL
comments.body: This is a hot topic, and I hear a ton of people saying that it should be allowed. People often believe in Karma, and that people should get what’s coming to them. While I do believe that people should be punished harshly for their crimes, I believe that everyone deserves to live. That is 100% not saying that I support what these criminals have done, but rather that I feel that people can change. I know that heavily optimistic and almost delusional, but I believe that people can come out as a whole new person after proper guidance. You were always taught as a kid that “two wrongs don’t make a right”. I believe that applies here as well. I especially feel that live-streaming the death of someone is incredibly wrong. Nobody should be able to turn on a channel and watch someone actually get killed.  There are kids out there who may have parents in prison, and those kids may be horrified at what is done, and may be done to their parents. Sure, some can argue that it shows people what will happen to criminals, but it doesn't make it any less morally challenged.

comments.body:
Fell into an early retirement (at greatly reduced rates) at 48. Spent the next 33 yrs living on the cheap, skiing, backpacking, hiking, mtn biking in CO mtns and UT desert. Worked odd jobs as needed. Aged out of those previous activities but now spend full days landscaping, gardening, exercising, stretching, meditating blah and blah. My to-do list is longer than I'll ever finish and I run out of time every day. I wake up the next day stoked to get at it. This is the most content I've ever felt despite the fact that Rich humans are making Ma Earth unlivable for Life As We Know It by overconsuming everything they can get their greedy hands on and Americans are so brain-dead that they elect full-on fascists who rob them blind. 

It's always NOW. Every moment is miracles within miracles. OM!

comments.name: Bruce Higgins
comments.body:
My dad retired, parked himself in a recliner, turned on the TV and basically didn't move. He was dead in 5 yrs.

With him as an example, when I retired I founded a homeless outreach team called "Old Farts With Hearts."  We are out feeding the homeless on the streets multiple times per week with food, water, clothing, and a kind word, the last being the most important thing we do.

To confirm to the people on the streets, "You are human, we see you, you matter, and we care." 

There are so many things that need fixing in our communities, be an Old Fart With a Heart and get involved.  It will give both you and the people you help the Warm Fuzzies.

comments.name: Kirk D
comments.body: My career was in the area of children's mental health.  Despite having to retire early five years ago at age 64 due to my declining health that was in part due to job related factors, I feel that I'm in a good place now.  I enjoy the free time and relative simplicity of retirement.  I have time to read which I very much enjoy and have good conversations with people without needing to keep checking the time.  Most of all, I have the time to actually see the amazing things in nature that are right in front of me that I might have walked past (or over) during busier times.   I also find mornings way more enjoyable in retirement and I'm reminded of a song (which I can't recall) that had the line, "Slow down you move too fast, you've got to make the morning last."  Add coffee...and retirement can be pretty good.

comments.name: Jenny
comments.body: The privilege embedded in this discussion is staggering. Blue-collar workers spend decades doing physically punishing work and die younger. For many, retirement isn’t a search for fulfillment; it’s relief from work that has worn down their bodies. The luxury of debating whether retirement provides enough purpose is itself a marker of class.

comments.name: Lorin Duckman
comments.body: I was mentally debilitated after being let go from a job which I took after being assassinated from a job as a Judge which had been a lifetime dream. We had already moved from NYC. Barely regained financial footing and lived in VT which was too expensive. I had opportunities to start up, but at 61, I couldn't start over again. My wife said time to be an artist, something you always wanted to be. Just promise me you will give up your law license and not go back. So, I enrolled at Champlain College, got a certificate in Graphic Design/digital media and then went on to photo school. By then, I was too old to be an intern or start a business. Did a few commissions. Entered a few contests. Taught a little. And, now, I have a vast portfolio of photos no one will buy, a small portrait studio that no one will sit in for a photo (free), and social media no one follows. 79. Very pleased with my wife and my photographic life and am prepared my end of life which will come sooner than later since I have blood cancer.

comments.name: Janey
comments.body: It depends what you’re retiring from. I’m a college professor. My job sustains me and I love it. My brother who works a blue collar construction job destroyed his body with hard physical labor and died at 65, before he was even able to retire.

comments.name: Unity Gain

At 73 I still write and record and produce music. I make videos for a You Tube channel I have. There is no money in this. But it does keep my mind active and it keeps me in touch with other musicians I get to play with. 

There is no beating Father Time but having something to do that you like and is fun makes being old so much better. 

Family and a group of freinds and acquiantances, no matter the size is also very important. Accept the good parts of being old and you will enjoy the latter years. I certainly do not miss working for money.

Before my job in a US school district, I worked in two middle schools in northern France for the 25-26 school year. The surveillant(e)s were a cornerstone of our school. If teachers had to send a kid out into the hall, if they had to take disciplinary action— basically, if the kids had to do anything outside the classroom/clubs, it was with a surveillant. I was (and am) so impressed by the amount of adults present in a French school building compared to Colorado, where teachers so often have to run from their classrooms to do lunch duty, only to run straight back again to continue teaching.
Our surveillants were beloved by the middle schoolers, because they were young (about half of them were getting their degrees to teach) and were able to joke around with the kids in a way that the teachers didn’t. They knew the kids’ hobbies, their unique social situations, their issues at home— just as well as the teachers did.
It breaks my heart to think of a surveillant using their position to hurt the kids they’re supposed to protect and care for, but how many other times have we seen some variation of this article with a different setting?
The Minister’s office needs to start treating the surveillants for what they are: an essential part of the school system. Stop paying them like they’re all 24 year-old master’s students, give them more hours or at least a set schedule, and then screen them like they’re applying for government security clearance. Sartorial Splendor

Knitting woolen mittens 
cost her a pittance, 
yet Molly obliged 
for her shivering kittens.

Then came four sox 
for her barefooted fox. 
Can’t forget underwear
for her lone, bashful bear. 
And two pairs of pants 
for each of her elephants. 

Leg warmers, of course,
for her zebra and horse. 
And a top hat and coat 
for her tap dancing goat. 

But when all the clothes 
were finally done,
every last penny
of Molly’s salary was gone.

Who can pay for this modest
circus sartorial splendor?
That bank-robbing Frank, 
her kind-hearted big spender!

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body:
Kelsey has about the biggest voice of any baritone in the business and does sing a lot of Verdi, so yes, he is definitely a Verdi baritone. But great? Maybe, but I'll have to hear a lot more. For the record, it is mentioned that he is 48 years old, but not that he has sung in only 13 Met seasons since 2007, and only 155 performances of 13 roles, 108 of them in 7 Verdi roles. Leonard Warren DIED at 48, and had sung 22 seasons in 657 performances of 26 roles, 372 of them in 12 Verdi roles. Some difference. For the record, and only taking into consideration American baritones from the 1950s on, and only their Met statistics, this may be of interest:

Name    Seasons   Roles  # of Perf.     Verdi Roles   # of Perf. 

Kelsey       13           23         155                  7                108
MacNeil     30          26          677               14                 392
Merrill        31           21         772                  8                491
Milnes        32          35          655               14                 392
Warren       22          26          657               12                 372

You can see the standard Kelsey is working against if anybody bothered to check it out. And while these baritones more or less ruled the Met baritone roster, they also had in-house competition from Valdengo, Bastianini, Sereni (500 performances), later Gobbi, even very late Taddei. Nucci, etc. Look at that list and tell me that Italian singing isn't now in a state of decline!

I ate in a dining shed – a fancy one with space heaters and the whole nine yards – exactly once. I couldn't square the feeling of pavement under my feet with the rest of the dining experience. It almost made the food taste off.

Shed the sheds. NYC never truly needed them and certainly doesn't need them now.

comments.name: JJ
comments.body:
I am surprised there is no mention that restaurant street sheds are coming back:

1. Proposal No. 1 of the Mayor’s November election proposals is to lessen City review and make it easier to building restaurant sheds on the street.

2. In August, the Mayor approved City Council legislation allow all-year restaurant street sheds (including winterizing them)

Besides all the evident issues (trash, rats, emergency vehicle impact. etc) with restaurant street sheds, here are a few more…

How is it OK for the City to allow these and block pedestrian visibility? 

Why is the City supporting restaurants by giving street space but not giving extra space to retail stores? 

How can the City insist that street cleaning-sweeping is essential and then allow these permanent structures which block street cleaning-sweeping?

comments.name: Kevin
comments.body: At the risk of sounding morbid - I always figured the final nail in the coffin for these would be a catastrophic traffic incident - while eating in these I always felt one drunk-driver away from getting totally plowed while sitting in one of the haphazard structures built within busy, narrow streets without any real safety considerations. I'm glad, to my knowledge, that never happened. These were charming and cool, like so many things in Covid - there's certain fondnessess to the Covid experience - although never far away from the reality of millions who died.

comments.name: R
comments.body: The sheds were of uneven quality, but I loved our experiment in reclaiming streets for the use and enjoyment of New Yorkers, rather than parked cars. It brought some liveliness our neighborhoods and gave us a glimpse of how Europeans use public space.  Why do drivers get to store their cars on the streets anyway - why is that the default in America’s densest area?

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: I don't understand how any of these could have been considered okay during covid as very few of them look as though they had adequate air circulation. In fact, I'm guessing the restaurants themselves, with higher ceilings and HVAC systems were more safe. Gross on many accounts (construction, rats, small spaces with too many people).

comments.name: David
comments.body: Outdoor dining sheds were part of the solution to eating at restaurants during the pandemic, in order to reduce the chance of becoming infected by breathing the air of folks with Covid. That time has passed and the downside of dining sheds in a traffic congested city with many narrow streets and sidewalks should be obvious. As is the huge problem of becoming a home to vermin, I'm looking at you, rats and roaches. Then there is also the issue of reduced parking, which has already been reduced by Citibike racks, alternate side of the street parking (which is supposed to be used for street cleaning but rarely is), widened curb cuts and other elimination of free parking. Unless you live here, you may not be aware that parking lots usually cost $50 - $80 for a couple of hours parking. Another issue is noise. You have to experience the amount of noise generated by outdoor dining under your window to appreciate how unpleasant this is. And, finally, there is the impracticality of the dining sheds. Sorry to burst your bubble, but they are usually either empty or hardly used. A lot of us City folk eat home nowadays, rather than pay exorbitant prices for usually substandard food.

comments.name: JB
comments.body: These sheds had a purpose...once...and had their day, but it's gone now.  Tear them all down!  Including the still-remaining, more permanent ones, which encroach on sidewalks and provide essentially rent-free space for some fancy restaurants.

comments.name: Retired attorney
comments.body: As a viewer with only rudimentary background knowledge about the Theranos scandal, I found this film to be delightful precisely because it had me "tied up in knots" the same way these critics describe. The magic of the film depends on there being an open question about whether Liz Holmes could genuinely believe herself to be innocent, a question the filmmakers raise by allowing that the entire Theranos debacle may have been nothing more than an Abbott-and-Costello-level misunderstanding about what the testing device could do. The attorney in me couldn't help but notice that the filmmakers never attempted to map out the full extent of the fraud; had they done so, I imagine, the central characters would have seemed far less complex and compelling.

comments.name: Stephen
comments.body:
I consider Nathan Fielder to be the millennial trickster god, but this film has me reconsidering that: is Fielder actually a great humanist artist? Part of the magic trick he's doing is showing that, actually, you CANNOT see everything--the interiority of another being is impossible to fully see, even for that being themself. And so this leads to making a distinction between "Truth," or the nature of "Reality," and honesty and trust. The questions of honesty and trust burrowed deep under my skin watching this.

SPOILER

Also, I am just enamored with Amanda Seyfried in this film! And Christopher Abbott! The Testament of Ann Lee was my favorite film last year, and to see them together for this one was a treat.

comments.name: Marc

As I watched this, I thought to myself, "Well, *someone* was there."
At the end, Nathan is relaying his conversation with Elizabeth (one which "we" weren't there). There is a line in the conversation which implicstes Elizabeth, and Nathan changes the line. Literally changes it in the script.
So ... did she really say that?
Amanda is again in the position of re-enacting dialogue which she can't know the truth of. Only this time the person making her do it is the one who contronted her about it earlier.
Their exhange echoes the clip from the teaser trailer. She asks if he's hiding something to protect Elizabeth. He replies, what reason would he have to lie?
.
Great movie.

It is my understanding that the IMF’s economic forecasts are often subject to frequent revisions and are not always considered the most reliable guide. I would not be surprised if their forecasts are drastically revised as we move forward.

However, one notable observation is that their predictions seem to indicate a substantial strengthening of the dollar in the foreseeable future. Because the U.S. is a net oil-exporting and energy self-sufficient nation, I believe it is in a much more stable position than much of the rest of the world, and this structural advantage will likely persist, strengthening the USD against the currencies of energy-dependent countries and potentially reinforcing the flight to the dollar safety phenomenon. This would likely significantly reduce inflationary pressure domestically and potentially require a sharp reversal in the Fed’s policies.

In my view, the Fed just cornered itself with its rushed decision to prematurely hike rates, only driving up costs without yielding any tangible benefits. The Fed should start a new round of small-scale QE to signal its intent to stabilize the bond market. This will swiftly lower bond yields, while any marginal inflationary pressure resulting from it could be effectively controlled and muted by raising short-term policy rates and adjusting the reserve requirement ratio. This would also allow the Fed to maintain its posturing of commitment to controlling inflation through consecutive rate hikes.

There's a practical problem with plain neutral framing of political arguments: it stops the media from advocating for truth and expertise.

When a reader is just tuning in, learning about a topic for the first time, they depend on the media to tell true expertise from complete bull. They don't yet have the independent knowledge to tell whether an argument actually reflects an expert perspective and what is utterly untrustworthy - and if two opinions are presented with equal weight, equal merit is the inference they will draw.

So if one political side is advocating for reality, but the other one simply lies, a naive reader will dismiss the entire argument as an unknown, like just a horse race. They will discard the issue, rather than "be the judge" as we might hope they do.

It's not enough to separately cover what expertise says in some different article, under some other headline, or to refer to articles from months or weeks prior. Readers deserve media that advocates for reality, repeatedly and as a first principle.

Not often mentioned...we often black-out in an outburst moment. The trigger hits, and poof! Black-out. You're gone.

Happened to me the other day. Not family, but work. normal, but nonetheless frustrating issue reared its head, I saw it pop-up and - I went ballistic. Later, I didn't have much sense or recall of the moment and realized I'd blacked-out. Such a thing had not happened to me in a very, very long time...

(I apologized to each person involved, or in the vicinity. I'm not too big, to not apologize.)
